newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 9.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 9.

text.p: THE DOMINION

Labour leader Helen Clark wants to form a coalition government with New Zealand First, but Clark says the appointment of Labour's Michael Cullen as finance minister would be non-negotiable in such a cabinet. That would rule out the appointment of New Zealand First leader Winston Peters to the post second only to the prime minister in power, a job insiders in his party have suggested he would want. Page 1.

Labour, Alliance, New Zealand First and other parties can throw in the towel - Tauranga Boys' College's three-yearly political poll has predicted a National-led government after October. In 24 years - eight elections - the school's "reflector poll" has never been wrong. Page 1.

National party president Geoff Thompson, trying to allay fears about a potential coalition with the Christian Coalition, promised voters National would not trade away its tradition as a "tolerant" party. Page 2.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters on Tuesday night named the strategic assets his party would restrict to 24.9 percent foreign ownership - including Telecom and Air New Zealand. They are Air New Zeland, all utilities, port companies, airport companies, all state-owned enterprises, market monopolies such as Telecom and Forestry Corporation. Page 2.

National Mutual's New Zealand policyholders saw their shares jump 18 percent on listing - opening with a bang at $2.00. About 137,000 New Zealand policyholders are now shareholders and the total share register in New Zealand should top 140,000. It will
be the biggest register of shareholders in New Zealand, ahead of Brierley Investments. Page 16.

Broking firms Direct Broking and ANZ Securities have been fined by the Stock Exchange over a trade in Strada shares at the time of Strada's capital reconstruction soon before delisting in March. A complaint by Strathmore Group, which tried to buy the shares that were cancelled, is still before the Securities Commission. Page 16.
Job ads fell 2.3 percent in September and 8.7 percent in the year to September, ANZ Bank said. Page 17.

Fertiliser co-operative SouthFert announced a $3.67 million profit for the year to June 30, down from $4.6 million last year. The co-operative is the subject of takeover offers from Ravensdown and BOP Fertiliser. Page 17.
Christchurch-based Pyne Gould Corporation increased its profit to $12.23 million for the year to June, up from last year's $8.21 million. Page 17.
Mercury Energy said it had organised a $390 million underwritten cash advance facility with a group of six banks. This is the second significant facility the company has obtained this year. Page 19.

The long-term implications of the single aviation market are enormous and extremely positive for Air New Zealand, Morgan Stanley says in a research report on Asian airlines. Specifically it argues that it would revive the development of a single aviation market. Such a market would be more flexible and efficient. Page 23.

Top business executives advising Asia-Pacific nations on setting up the world's biggest free trade zone are becoming impatient with the slow rate of progress and want political leaders to share their sense of urgency. Page 25.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters has dropped the biggest hint yet that Labour is his preferred coalition partner. In a speech yesterday, he outlined social policy areas on which he expected a coalition to be negotiated. Peters said New Zealand First had matched their policies on social, economic and fiscal issues against Labour's and National's. "It is clear the Labour Party's current social manifesto policies are closer to that of New Zealand First's than National's." Page 1.

Labour leader Helen Clark doubts Maori support for New Zealand First is as strong in Maori electorates as the Winston-Peters led party would have Maori believe. Clark said she believed New Zealand First support was declining among Maori in tandem with the party's popularity slide in the polls.

TVNZ has rejected as a probable hoax claims that its "worm jockeys" could be biased. A caller to Newstalk ZB said he and his wife were not asked about their political leanings when selected for the panel of 120 uncommitted voters used in Monday night's leaders debate. TVNZ's head of news Shaun Brown said he
was sceptical about the call. He said Colmar Brunton had a long list of questions designed to detect people's political preferences.

Around a quarter of a billion dollars has flowed into the New Zealand household sector following yesterday's successful float of insurer National Mutual. The shares reached 204 cents before closing at 201 cent in heavy trade on the New Zealand Stock Exchange.

The sweetened offer by the Dublin-based Independent Newspapers for Wilson and Horton might have softened opposition to the takeover bid but it still could find it hard to get to 100 percent. It is estimated as much as 10 percent of the Wilson and Horton share register might be held by investors unwilling to sell at virtually any price. One broker said history had shown Wilson and Horton shareholders were extremely long-term investors.

New Zealand fund managers are unrattled by suggestions that world sharemarkets are overheating. On Monday, New York's Dow Jones share index topped 6000 for the first time while German DAX index set yet another record at 2,702. London pension fund manager Tony Dye has amassed a cash mountain of $16 billion in expectation of a 1987-style worldwide crash. A more circumspect International Monetary Fund warned recently the United States economy may be in danger of overheating.
Queensland-based Mackay Refined Sugars is to sue New Zealand Sugar Corporation in New Zealand's High Court in the latest bid to secure market share.
The bout of pre-election nerves now driving the New Zealand dollar lower and boosting bond yields on financial markets is totally unnecessary, according to the Union Bank of Switzerland.
